newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy treasury attacked over Telcom share decision.
newsitem.headline: Italy treasury attacked over Telcom share decision.

text.p: Investors are up in arms over the Treasury's handling of a decision not to allow them to convert savings shares in Stet and Telecom Italia SpA into ordinary shares in the companies, which are being merged ahead of privatisation later in the year.

Sources with brokerage houses in Milan and London said that a conference call with Treasury officials on Tuesday had failed to pacify investors, some of whom feel they should have been given advance warning of the Treasury's intentions.
Three fund managers, two of them U.S.-based and one British were writing to the Treasury to lodge a protest, an equities analyst in the Milan office of an investment bank said.

Shares in Stet and Telecom Italia, which are merging into a single group next month, plunged on Monday, the first day of trading after the Treasury announced there would be no conversion. Shares have since stabilised.

Many investors both in Italy and overseas had bought savings shares, which pay a higher dividend than ordinary stock, in both companies in anticipation they would be able to profit by converting them into voting shares.

Brokers contacted by Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity, said many were aware there was an element of risk attached to investing in the savings shares on the assumption they could later be converted into ordinary stock.
"It was always a fifty-fifty bet and it could have gone either way," said a London-based equity sales executive.
"Anyone who led their clients to believe it was a done deal was leading them up the garden path."

Savings shares in Italy traditionally trade at a discount of up to 35 percent to ordinary shares. The discount between Stet and Telecom saving and ordinary shares narrowed sharply in recent months as investors piled into the market.

Treasury Director General Mario Draghi told fund managers in yesterday's conference call that the Treasury decided not to allow conversion because it feared the value of ordinary shares would have fallen as a result, a share analyst who listened in on the call said.
Draghi said the Treasury was also concerned that, if it had allowed the conversion to go ahead, liquidity would have been drained from the market.
Investors were allowed to convert savings shares in Banca Commerciale Italiana and Credito Italiano into ordinary stock when the two banks were privatised in 1994.
But investors had to pay to convert the shares under a formula taking into account the higher dividends they had received while holders of savings stock.
If the same formula had been applied to a Stet share conversion the telecoms group would have gained up to 1.3 trillion lire ($800 million), analysts said.

Some analysts believe the real reason the Treasury opposed conversion was that an increased pool of voting shares could make it harder to assemble a core of friendly shareholders in the company when it is fully privatised.
The Treasury could have taken preemptive action to save investors from being wrongfooted, brokers said.
"The Treasury could have put out a statement many months ago saying that warning investors that they could not count on the shares being converted," said a Milan equities salesman.
"To allow a stock to get into a situation where one piece of news moves it by 15 percent is not wise. The market wants to be given news a little at a time," he added.
